title: Any Peak
statement_md:
A trail profile lists the heights of consecutive markers, and **no two neighbouring markers have the same height**. A marker is a **peak** when it's higher than each neighbour it has: the first and last markers have only one neighbour to beat.

Return the position of **any** peak. There is always at least one, and every peak is an accepted answer.

A scan finds one in linear time. Can you find one while looking at only $O(\log n)$ heights?
constraints: $1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^4$, where $n$ is the number of markers

solutions.title: Walk Until the First Descent
solutions.intuition_md: Walk the trail from the left. As long as each step goes up, the marker behind you beat its left neighbour. The first time a step goes **down**, the marker you're on beat both sides: it's a peak. If the trail never goes down, the last marker is a peak.
solutions.algorithm_md: For `i` from `0` to `n - 2`: if `heights[i] > heights[i + 1]`, return `i`. After the loop, return `n - 1`.
solutions.time_complexity_reason: One pass in the worst case (a trail that only rises).

solutions.title: Climb by Halving
solutions.intuition_md: Look at any marker `mid` and its right neighbour. If the trail rises from `mid` to `mid + 1`, keep walking uphill to the right: the heights can't rise forever, so the first descent after `mid` (or the end of the trail) is a peak on that side. If it falls instead, the same argument walking left from `mid` puts a peak at `mid` or to its left. Either way one comparison rules out half the range while keeping a peak inside it.
solutions.algorithm_md:
1. `lo = 0`, `hi = n - 1`. Invariant: a peak lies in `[lo, hi]`.
2. While `lo < hi`: take `mid = (lo + hi) / 2`. If `heights[mid] < heights[mid + 1]`, set `lo = mid + 1`; otherwise set `hi = mid`.
3. When `lo == hi`, the range holds exactly one marker, and the invariant says it's a peak.
